# Using uv in pre-commit

An official pre-commit hook is provided at `astral-sh/uv-pre-commit`.

To use uv with pre-commit, add one of the following examples to the `repos` list in the `.pre-commit-config.yaml`.

To make sure your `uv.lock` file is up to date even if your `pyproject.toml` file was changed:

.pre-commit-config.yaml

```
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    # uv version.
    rev: 0.13.0
    hooks:
      - id: uv-lock

```

To keep a `requirements.txt` file in sync with your `uv.lock` file:

.pre-commit-config.yaml

```
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    # uv version.
    rev: 0.13.0
    hooks:
      - id: uv-export

```

To compile requirements files:

.pre-commit-config.yaml

```
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    # uv version.
    rev: 0.13.0
    hooks:
      # Compile requirements
      - id: pip-compile
        args: [requirements.in, -o, requirements.txt]

```

To compile alternative requirements files, modify `args` and `files`:

.pre-commit-config.yaml

```
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    # uv version.
    rev: 0.13.0
    hooks:
      # Compile requirements
      - id: pip-compile
        args: [requirements-dev.in, -o, requirements-dev.txt]
        files: ^requirements-dev\.(in|txt)$

```

To run the hook over multiple files at the same time, add additional entries:

.pre-commit-config.yaml

```
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    # uv version.
    rev: 0.13.0
    hooks:
      # Compile requirements
      - id: pip-compile
        name: pip-compile requirements.in
        args: [requirements.in, -o, requirements.txt]
      - id: pip-compile
        name: pip-compile requirements-dev.in
        args: [requirements-dev.in, -o, requirements-dev.txt]
        files: ^requirements-dev\.(in|txt)$

```

results.title: Astral releases uv 0.13.0 with eight breaking changes: Reveneau
results.text:
Astral releases uv 0.13.0 with eight breaking changes: Reveneau

# Astral releases uv 0.13.0 with eight breaking changes

Astral released uv 0.13.0 with eight breaking changes, including Python 3.15 as the default stable version, strict hash validation in included constraints files, and a new tar backend that rejects some older archives.

Editorial 4 days ago 2 min read

Why it matters A team pinning uv in CI needs to read the eight breaking changes before upgrading, because a build that passed on 0.12 can now fail on a hash check, an older archive, or a changed path parse.

A Python team that pinned uv at 0.12 and ran `uv sync` every morning now has eight reasons to read release notes before upgrading. Astral released uv 0.13.0, the version Astral itself labels with eight breaking changes.

The first change is the default stable Python. uv 0.13.0 downloads CPython 3.15 when no version is pinned, where 0.12 downloaded 3.14. A project with no version pinned, including anything that calls `uv run` on a bare script, will now resolve against a different interpreter than it did on the previous release. CPython 3.15.0 was added in the same release.

## The seven other breaks, in plain words

Astral says uv now honours `--require-hashes` in constraints files pulled in with `-c`, where the directive was ignored before. An installation that worked on 0.12 can fail here if any included constraint sets the flag and any requirement is missing a hash. In the same category, uv now rejects editable (`-e`) requirements in a constraints file instead of silently dropping them, which Astral says matches pip's behaviour.

On Windows ARM64 machines, uv now prefers native `aarch64` interpreters where it picked an emulated x86_64 before. The fallback is still there, so a project that depends on an x86-only wheel is not broken, but a build that happened to pick an emulated interpreter will switch architectures on the next run without any flag change.

Three more changes are smaller but can still break a build. uv 0.13.0 switches its tar backend from `astral-tokio-tar` to `tar-codec`, which Astral says applies stricter validation and will reject some archives the old backend accepted. Options such as `--constraint` now treat each value as a single path rather than splitting on spaces, so a path with a space in it works now and two paths on one flag do not. `uv build --clear` now refuses to delete an output directory that contains a build source, which blocks a class of accidents where the clear step removes the project files.

The eighth change is about Python startup. uv no longer writes `_virtualenv.py` and `_virtualenv.pth` into virtual environments on Python 3.10 or newer, which Astral says reduces Python startup overhead. The patch stays for 3.9 and earlier.

## One preview, and the usual performance notes

The 0.13.0 release adds a preview `--require-build-hashes` flag, which extends the hash requirement to the packages a project builds against rather than only the packages it installs. Astral lists four performance improvements alongside the breaking changes: HTTP response revalidation, fewer allocations in cached response handling, smaller cache storage for policy and record data, and fewer allocations in cached source distribution revisions.

Astral does not state why these changes land in 0.13 rather than another 0.12 patch, and no migration guide is linked from the release page. The notes themselves list the breaking changes with the exact option names and file paths that trigger each one, which is where a team upgrading in CI should start.

## Source

Astral.

This item was written by an AI system from the linked source. Reveneau is responsible for what it publishes.

# Fix uv 0.13.0 sdist hard links: the tarball is legal

 By Indra Gusti Prasetya October 13, 2026 10 min read 

Audit uv.lock for sdists with hard-link members before upgrading: uv 0.13.0's new tar backend rejects them, and only on a cold cache.

uv 0.13.0 replaced the tar implementation underneath every archive uv reads, and the release notes say so in one line: "uv may now reject archives containing hard links or unsupported tar extensions that previous versions accepted." A dependency that resolved, downloaded and built on 0.12.24 can stop installing on 0.13.0 with the same lockfile and the same pinned hash, and the archive is not corrupt. By the end of this you will have a script that reads `uv.lock`, pulls every source distribution it pins and names the ones carrying a hard-link member, a local reproduction that needs no network, and three fixes ordered by how long you can leave them in place.

The release note announcing the change enumerates nothing: no affected packages, no error-string reference, and the opt-out environment variable landed in the same release. The mechanism has to be read out of the backend crate, which is most of the work below. uv's archive layer has produced this class of surprise before, as in the 0.12.14 symlinked-directory rejection.

This one will come back

Package managers ship breaking changes on their own schedule, and the error text is never in the release notes. I read those notes as they land and write the fix the day it starts breaking builds.

## Prerequisites

- uv 0.13.0 on the machine under test (`uv --version`). A standalone-installer uv moves with `uv self update`; a pip-installed or Homebrew uv has to be upgraded through that package manager.
- Python 3.11 or newer for the audit script. It uses `tomllib`, which entered the standard library in 3.11.
- A project with a committed `uv.lock`.
- GNU tar if you intend to repack an archive (`tar --version`), for the `--hard-dereference` flag.
- The ability to run with a cold cache, because that is the only condition under which the new policy executes.

Hold onto one fact before you blame a package author. The PyPA source distribution format spec allows links in an sdist. It forbids only "Links (symbolic or hard) pointing outside the destination directory," and it tells tools they "MAY unpack links (symbolic or hard) as regular files, using content from the archive." A stricter client is weak evidence about the artifact, which was also the situation when Terraform 1.16.3 started rejecting binary/octet-stream downloads that were perfectly good zips.

### 1. Confirm the backend changed under you

```
uv --version
uv cache dir
```

PR #22094, "Use tar-codec by default", removed the crate's preview flag and routed extraction, `uv_build` sdist creation and `uv publish` metadata reads through it. The crate is `tar-codec`, part of astral-sh/astral-codec, whose README still carries the line: "This repository is in a very early state of development and is not considered ready for production use." That is the component now opening every tarball uv touches.

### 2. List every sdist your lockfile pins

```
# scan_sdists.py
import tomllib, sys

lock = tomllib.load(open("uv.lock", "rb"))
for pkg in lock.get("package", []):
    sdist = pkg.get("sdist")
    if sdist and "url" in sdist:
        print(pkg["name"], pkg["version"], sdist["url"], sep="\t")
```

```
python3 scan_sdists.py | tee sdists.tsv | wc -l
```

Each `[[package]]` table in `uv.lock` carries an optional `sdist = { url, hash, size }`. Packages resolved to a wheel have no `sdist` key and cannot hit this failure, so the first pass usually cuts the surface down to a handful of rows.

### 3. Classify the members of each archive

```
# audit_tars.py
import io, sys, tarfile, urllib.request

OK = {tarfile.REGTYPE, tarfile.AREGTYPE, tarfile.DIRTYPE, tarfile.SYMTYPE}

for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
    name, version, url

# uv 0.13 and Ruff 0.17: pin the defaults before upgrading

Published 10/10/2026 Repo astral-sh/uv

Pin the interpreter and lint target before upgrading; a successful dependency install does not prove the runtime stayed the same.

Python environments and code checks underpin agent tools, evaluations and scheduled jobs. Changing their defaults can change a fresh deployment without changing application code.

## What changed

uv 0.13.0, released on 9 October, moves its default stable Python from 3.14 to 3.15. Ruff 0.17.0, released the same day, changes its own Python and lint defaults. These are released versions, not just commits on the default branch.

The uv distinction matters: it does not automatically replace every existing interpreter with 3.15. Compatible installed interpreters can still be used. An unversioned `uv python install`, or a command that needs to download a suitable interpreter, can now select 3.15. A fresh runner and a long-lived development machine may therefore behave differently.

There are other operational changes in 0.13.0:

- `--require-hashes` inside a constraints file included from a requirements file is now honoured. Installs that previously passed may fail when hashes are missing.
- Editable requirements inside those included constraints files are rejected rather than silently ignored. They belong in requirements or explicit `--editable` arguments.
- Requirement-file options such as `--constraint` now treat their value as one path. Repeat the option for multiple files instead of supplying a quoted space-separated list.
- The default tar backend changes to `tar-codec`, with stricter archive validation. Some archives accepted before may be rejected; source distributions built with `uv_build` can have different bytes and hashes.
- Cache formats change. Dependencies may need to be downloaded or rebuilt after the upgrade, although different uv versions can safely share the cache directory.
- `uv build --clear` now rejects output directories containing a build source, including equivalent paths through symlinks, before clearing them. That is a useful safeguard against deleting the input.

Ruff’s changes are separate from uv’s interpreter selection. With no configured target or inferred project requirement, Ruff now defaults to a Python 3.11 target rather than 3.10. Its unconfigured syntax checking moves to Python 3.15. Neither setting installs an interpreter.

Several datetime rules leave Ruff’s default rule set, while `F406` enters it. Trailing pragma comments are handled consistently across formatting and the affected lint rules, which can produce formatting changes. macOS and Windows binaries in release archives and wheels are now code-signed.

The companion Ruff VS Code 2026.86.0 release removes legacy `ruff-lsp` support and passes `--untrusted-workspace` to the native server for untrusted workspaces.

## Why it matters

A package-manager upgrade can become a runtime upgrade on a fresh machine. That is the risk worth paying attention to here, rather than assuming a new version makes agents faster or more capable.

For Foundry jobs, Hermes-related Python tooling, or Python helpers around an OpenClaw deployment, the relevant question is simple: is the interpreter actually pinned, or has the existing machine been hiding an implicit default? This is a deployment concern, not a claim that either agent framework requires or supports Python 3.15.

The constraints fixes also expose configurations that previously appeared to work because uv ignored part of them. A new missing-hash error is not a reason to switch off hash checking reflexively. Check whether the requirement was intended to be enforced, then supply the missing hashes.

Ruff adds another source of drift. Fewer datetime warnings after an upgrade may reflect changed defaults, not improved code. For scheduled jobs, dropping timezone checks without noticing is particularl

# uv

 
 
 

An extremely fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Installing Trio 's dependencies with a warm cache. 
 

## Highlights

- A single tool to replace `pip`, `pip-tools`, `pipx`, `poetry`, `pyenv`, `twine`, `virtualenv`, and
 more.
- 10-100x faster than `pip`.
- Provides comprehensive project management, with a
 universal lockfile.
- Runs scripts, with support for
 inline dependency metadata.
- Installs and manages Python versions.
- Runs and installs tools published as Python packages.
- Includes a pip-compatible interface for a performance boost with a familiar
 CLI.
- Supports Cargo-style workspaces for
 scalable projects.
- Disk-space efficient, with a global cache for
 dependency deduplication.
- Installable without Rust or Python via `curl` or `pip`.
- Supports macOS, Linux, and Windows.

uv is backed by Astral, the creators of
Ruff and ty.

## Installation

Install uv with our standalone installers:

```bash
# On macOS and Linux.
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

```bash
# On Windows.
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Or, from PyPI:

```bash
# With pip.
pip install uv
```

```bash
# Or pipx.
pipx install uv
```

If installed via the standalone installer, uv can update itself to the latest version:

```bash
uv self update
```

See the installation documentation for
details and alternative installation methods.

## Documentation

uv's documentation is available at docs.astral.sh/uv.

Additionally, the command line reference documentation can be viewed with `uv help`.

## Features

### Projects

uv manages project dependencies and environments, with support for lockfiles, workspaces, and more,
similar to `rye` or `poetry`:

```console
$ uv init example
Initialized project `example` at `/home/user/example`

$ cd example

$ uv add ruff
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 2 packages in 170ms
   Built example @ file:///home/user/example
Prepared 2 packages in 627ms
Installed 2 packages in 1ms
 + example==0.1.0 (from file:///home/user/example)
 + ruff==0.5.0

$ uv run ruff check
All checks passed!

$ uv lock
Resolved 2 packages in 0.33ms

$ uv sync
Resolved 2 packages in 0.70ms
Checked 1 package in 0.02ms
```

See the project documentation to get started.

uv also supports building and publishing projects, even if they're not managed with uv. See the
publish guide to learn more.

### Scripts

uv manages dependencies and environments for single-file scripts.

Create a new script and add inline metadata declaring its dependencies:

```console
$ echo 'import requests; print(requests.get("https://astral.sh"))' > example.py

$ uv add --script example.py requests
Updated `example.py`
```

Then, run the script in an isolated virtual environment:

```console
$ uv run example.py
Reading inline script metadata from: example.py
Installed 5 packages in 12ms
<Response [200]>
```

See the scripts documentation to get started.

# Panduan uv (1): Instalasi dan Manajemen Versi Python

 Juhyun Lee termasuk dalam Python 2026-10-11 Sekitar 1600 kata 8 menit 

# Ikhtisar 

uv adalah alat pengelola paket dan proyek Python yang dibuat oleh Astral dengan Rust. Mulai dari menginstal Python, membuat virtual environment, menginstal paket, mengunci dependensi, hingga menjalankan alat baris perintah, semuanya ditangani dengan satu perintah, dan yang terpenting, uv sangat cepat. Di seri ini, kita akan mempelajari cara memakai uv satu per satu beserta contohnya. Di bagian pertama ini, kita akan menginstal uv dan mengelola versi Python.

## Alat yang Digantikan uv 

| Pekerjaan | Alat yang biasa dipakai | uv |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Menginstal dan berganti versi Python | pyenv | `uv python` |
| Membuat virtual environment | venv, virtualenv | `uv venv` (otomatis di dalam proyek) |
| Menginstal paket | pip | `uv pip`, `uv add` |
| Mengunci versi dependensi | pip-tools, Poetry | `uv lock`, `uv.lock` |
| Menginstal dan menjalankan alat baris perintah | pipx | `uv tool`, `uvx` |

Python 3.15

 October 9, 2026

##### Brent Westbrook

@ntBre

Python 3.15, the next stable version of Python, is available now, along with new versions of Ruff, uv, and ty!

To get started, update uv, upgrade to Python 3.15, and install the latest versions of Ruff and ty:

```
uv self update
uv python upgrade 3.15
uv tool install ruff@latest
uv tool install ty@latest
```

Python 3.15 includes many exciting new features. We've chosen some of our favorites to describe below, along with related changes in our tools.

## Lazy imports #

Python 3.15 introduces a new `lazy` keyword that can be used to defer loading of imports, avoiding the cost of importing modules until they are actually needed. In many cases, lazy imports can replace both function-local and `TYPE_CHECKING` imports that were used to defer expensive imports, allowing you to keep more imports in one block at the top of a file, as recommended by PEP 8. As long as the imports aren't actually used at runtime, they won't be loaded immediately.

You can get a taste for how lazy imports work with a brief REPL session. Regular imports immediately install their modules in `sys.modules`, while lazy imports instead appear only in `sys.lazy_modules` until their first runtime usage. 1 Note that the annotation for `x` does not count as a runtime usage because of the deferred annotation semantics introduced in Python 3.14.

```
>>> import sys
>>> import json
>>> 'json' in sys.modules
True
>>> lazy import tomllib
>>> # Accessing `tomllib` in an annotation does not load the module
>>> x: tomllib.TOMLDecodeError
>>> 'tomllib' in sys.modules
False
>>> 'tomllib' in sys.lazy_modules
True
>>> # Using `tomllib` at runtime finally loads the module
>>> tomllib.loads("tool.ruff.target-version = 'py315'")
{'tool': {'ruff': {'target-version': 'py315'}}}
>>> 'tomllib' in sys.modules
True
```

Ruff v0.17 stabilizes two new rules to help you manage your lazy imports and updates existing rules to respect import laziness. First, `lazy-import-mismatch` (`TID254`) allows you to configure lists of imports that should always be lazy or never be lazy and enforce this in your project. For example, with the following configuration:

```
[lint.flake8-tidy-imports]
ban-lazy = ["json"]
require-lazy = ["typing"]
```

`TID254` would be emitted on both of these imports:

```
lazy from json import loads  # TID254: `json` should be imported eagerly
import typing  # TID254: `typing` should be imported lazily
```

Both diagnostics come with an autofix to apply the correct laziness. For convenience, `ban-lazy` and `require-lazy` also recognize a special `all` selector. See their documentation for more details.

Second, `lazy-import-immediately-resolved` (`TID255`) helps to identify cases where a nominally lazy import is actually loaded eagerly, defeating the purpose of marking it lazy. For example, using `foo.Bar` as a base class causes the `foo` module to be loaded:

```
lazy import foo

class C(foo.Bar): ...
```

It would typically require substantial restructuring to avoid using such an import eagerly, so the rule offers a fix to remove `lazy` from the import to make its immediate use clearer.

For projects that support older Python versions in addition to 3.15, PEP 810 also introduced the `__lazy_modules__` global variable. A definition like the following:

```
__lazy_modules__ = ["typing"]

import typing
```

has the same effect as `lazy import typing` but without using new syntax that would be rejected by older Python versions. Ruff recognizes both forms as well.

In addition to these new rules, `typing-only-first-party-import` (`TC001`), `typing-only-third-party-import` (`TC002`), and `typing-only-standard-library-import` (`TC003`) have also been updated both to recognize lazy imports as an alternative to `TYPE_CHECKING` blocks and to recommend using them on Python 3.15 and later.

# Building distributions

To distribute your project to others (e.g., to upload it to an index like PyPI), you'll need to build it into a distributable format.

Python projects are typically distributed as both source distributions (sdists) and binary distributions (wheels). The former is typically a `.tar.gz` or `.zip` file containing the project's source code along with some additional metadata, while the latter is a `.whl` file containing pre-built artifacts that can be installed directly.

Important

When using `uv build`, uv acts as a build frontend and only determines the Python version to use and invokes the build backend. The details of the builds, such as the included files and the distribution filenames, are determined by the build backend, as defined in `[build-system]`. Information about build configuration can be found in the respective tool's documentation.

## Using `uv build`

`uv build` can be used to build both source distributions and binary distributions for your project. By default, `uv build` will build the project in the current directory, and place the built artifacts in a `dist/` subdirectory:

```
$ uv build
$ ls dist/
example-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
example-0.1.0.tar.gz

```

You can build the project in a different directory by providing a path to `uv build`, e.g., `uv build path/to/project`.

`uv build` will first build a source distribution, and then build a binary distribution (wheel) from that source distribution.

You can limit `uv build` to building a source distribution with `uv build --sdist`, a binary distribution with `uv build --wheel`, or build both distributions from source with `uv build --sdist --wheel`.

## Build constraints

`uv build` accepts `--build-constraint`, which can be used to constrain the versions of any build requirements during the build process. When coupled with `--require-hashes`, uv will enforce that the requirement used to build the project match specific, known hashes, for reproducibility.

For example, given the following `constraints.txt`:

```
setuptools==68.2.2 --hash=sha256:b454a35605876da60632df1a60f736524eb73cc47bbc9f3f1ef1b644de74fd2a

```

Running the following would build the project with the specified version of `setuptools`, and verify that the downloaded `setuptools` distribution matches the specified hash:

```
$ uv build --build-constraint constraints.txt --require-hashes

```

To require hashes for every build dependency, including transitive dependencies, use `--require-build-hashes` instead.

### Project build dependency hashes

For example, to verify build dependencies during project resolution and installation, add hashes to `build-constraint-dependencies` in your workspace's `pyproject.toml`:

```
[tool.uv]
build-constraint-dependencies = [
    { requirement = "setuptools==68.2.2", hashes = ["sha256:b454a35605876da60632df1a60f736524eb73cc47bbc9f3f1ef1b644de74fd2a"] },
    "wheel<1",
]

```

uv checks supplied hashes when it downloads pinned build dependencies. Constraints without hashes, such as `wheel<1`, are also allowed. To require a hash for every build dependency, including transitive dependencies, set `require-build-hashes = true` under `[tool.uv]` or pass `--require-build-hashes`.

You'll need to pin each build dependency to an exact version (or use a direct URL) and provide a hash. Hashes can also come from URL fragments in `build-system.requires`, but not from requirements returned by a build backend.

When build isolation is disabled, uv uses the installed build dependencies without checking their hashes. uv also does not recheck already-installed packages or previously built wheels. The bundled `uv_build` backend does not need a hash because it is part of the uv executable.

Note

`--require-build-hashes` is experimental. Use `--preview-features build-dependency-hashes` to suppress the warning.

# uv previews workflows driven by a lockfile without a workspace manifest

uv 0.12.23 extends frozen-lockfile preview workflows and fixes dependency-source conflicts and Windows emulation wheel selection.

Published: 2026-10-04

## What happened

Astral released uv 0.12.23 on 2026-10-03. Its frozen-lockfile preview expands what developers can do with uv.lock when the workspace manifest is absent: synchronize an environment, export dependencies, inspect a dependency tree and read workspace metadata. The release separately adds CPython 3.15.0rc3 and addresses installation correctness on Windows ARM64. The manifest-free commands remain preview features and require the stated frozen-lockfile mode.

## Key facts

- ✔ Astral released uv 0.12.23 on 2026-10-03.
- ✔ The release adds CPython 3.15.0rc3.
- ✔ The frozen-lockfile preview lets uv sync --frozen synchronize from uv.lock without a workspace manifest.
- ✔ With the frozen-lockfile preview, uv export --frozen and uv tree --frozen can export requirements and inspect dependency trees from uv.lock without a workspace manifest.
- ✔ The preview lets uv workspace metadata --frozen inspect workspace metadata and optionally synchronize the environment from uv.lock without a workspace manifest.
- ✔ uv rejects alternative sources for workspace members across conflicting dependency selections to avoid lockfiles that cannot be installed.
- ✔ On Windows ARM64, x86-64 Python interpreters running under emulation can install compatible win_amd64 wheels rather than build from source.

## Why it matters

The practical benefit is a simpler separation between a resolved dependency snapshot and the original workspace files. For build and deployment workflows that already carry a lockfile, the preview provides more ways to inspect or reconstruct that environment without reconstructing the full manifest layout. The source-conflict fix addresses correctness, while compatible wheel selection can avoid unnecessary source builds under emulation. These implications follow from the documented behavior; the release does not provide a general performance benchmark.

## Background

The announcement separates preview functionality from ordinary bug fixes and Python-version availability. Each manifest-free operation is explicitly paired with a frozen command and the frozen-lockfile preview. The Windows change specifically concerns x86-64 Python running under emulation and compatible win_amd64 wheels, rather than a claim that every package now has a native Windows ARM64 build.
